hello.note: Said with palms pressed together and a slight nod, to anyone, at any time. Also goodbye

how-are-you.note: To a man. To a woman, कैसी (KAI-see). आप (aap) is the polite you

im-well.note: The same for a man or a woman. The th is a t with a puff of air, not the English th

good-morning.note: Formal and a little bookish. Most people simply say नमस्ते, or good morning in English

good-night.note: Formal. Good night in English is common too

goodbye.note: Literally "we'll meet again". नमस्ते works for goodbye too

please.note: Rather formal. Hindi is polite through आप (aap) and verbs ending in -iye, such as दीजिए (DEE-ji-ye), please give

thank-you.note: शुक्रिया (shuk-REE-yaa) is just as common. Close friends and family rarely say thank you

yes.note: जी (jee) makes it polite. The famous head wobble often means yes or OK

no.note: नहीं, धन्यवाद (na-HEEN, DHAN-ya-vaad) is no, thank you

excuse-me.note: Sorry, and excuse me to get attention. सुनिए (SU-ni-ye), listen please, also calls a waiter

my-name.note: The name goes in the middle: the verb comes last. The audio uses Peter as the example name

your-name.note: Polite and the same for anyone

where-from.note: Answer मैं ... से हूँ (main ... se hoon), I'm from...

dont-understand.note: Literally "understanding didn't come to me", the same for a man or a woman

speak-english.note: To a man. To a woman, बोलती (BOL-tee). English is widely spoken in cities and anywhere tourists go

thousand.note: Prices are in rupees, रुपये (ru-PA-ye), written ₹

hundred-thousand.note: A lakh, written 1,00,000: India groups big numbers in lakhs and crores (a crore is 100 lakh, ten million)

million.note: Ten lakh. There is no everyday word for a million

how-much.note: Literally "for how much is this?" Point at the thing

would-like.note: Literally "to me ... is needed", the usual polite way to ask, the same for a man or a woman. The audio uses एक चाय (ek chaai), a tea

i-want.note: Literally "please give ...", a polite request. The audio uses यह वाला (YE waa-laa), this one

do-you-have.note: Literally "is ... near you?" The audio uses पानी (PAA-nee), water

discount.note: Literally "make it a little less". Bargaining is expected in markets and with auto-rickshaws, not in shops with printed prices

card.note: Bigger shops take cards. Most people pay by phone with UPI, which visitors can use with some apps; carry cash too

reservation.note: Booking, from English, is the usual word

taxi.note: Literally "please call a taxi". Ola and Uber are everywhere in cities, for cars and auto-rickshaws

train.note: Indian Railways is huge: book ahead on the IRCTC website or app

airport.note: Airport, in English, is understood everywhere

which-train.text: ... के लिए कौन सी ट्रेन है?
which-train.say: ... ke li-ye KAUN see tren hai
which-train.note: Literally "for ..., which train is it?" The place comes first. The audio uses आगरा (AA-graa), Agra
which-train.spoken: आगरा के लिए कौन सी ट्रेन है?
which-train.filled: ⟦आगरा⟧ के लिए कौन सी ट्रेन है?

buy-ticket.note: Literally "where will I get a ticket?"

two-tickets.note: The audio uses Agra as the example
two-tickets.spoken: आगरा के लिए दो टिकट दीजिए

trip-length.note: The audio uses Agra as the example
trip-length.spoken: आगरा पहुँचने में कितना समय लगेगा?

delicious.note: Many people say बहुत टेस्टी (ba-HUT TES-tee), very tasty

allergic.note: The same for a man or a woman. Add the food: मूँगफली (MOONG-pha-lee) peanuts, मेवे (ME-ve) nuts, अंडे (AN-de) eggs. The audio uses peanuts

love-dish.text: मुझे यह खाना बहुत पसंद आया!
love-dish.say: MU-jhe ye KHAA-naa ba-HUT pa-SAND AA-yaa
love-dish.note: Literally "this food pleased me a lot", the same for anyone

what-called.note: Point at the dish or item

table-for-two.text: दो लोगों के लिए टेबल चाहिए
table-for-two.say: do LO-gon ke li-ye TE-bal CHAA-hi-ye
table-for-two.note: For more people: तीन (teen), 3, or चार (chaar), 4

beer.note: Some states, such as Gujarat and Bihar, are dry. Elsewhere, look for a bar or a licensed restaurant

coffee.note: In the south, ask for filter coffee, strong and milky

tea.note: Usually masala chai: milky, sweet, and spiced, sold at every corner

sugar.note: Tea comes sweet. Without sugar is बिना चीनी (bi-NAA CHEE-nee)

hot.note: Hot, and hot weather. Spicy is तीखा (TEE-khaa); ask for कम तीखा (kam TEE-khaa), less spicy

cheers.note: The English word is the usual toast

help.note: Shout it. For any emergency, call 112

need-doctor.note: The same for a man or a woman. For an ambulance, call 108 or 112

pharmacy.note: Literally "the medicine shop". Chemist, in English, is widely understood
